analysis.one_liner: Repeals the federal estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer taxes.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with no cosponsors, never advanced past a committee referral and died when the 106th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would eliminate the federal estate tax and gift tax, including the tax on generation-skipping transfers, for anyone dying or making a transfer after enactment [S2, S3]. The estate tax applies only to the largest inherited fortunes; repealing it would cut federal revenue that otherwise comes from those estates [S2]. The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced and no further action was ever taken [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Heirs of the largest estates — the tax applies only to estates above the filing threshold, so the benefit is concentrated among a small number of very wealthy families. Estate-planning professionals would lose business as the need for sheltering structures disappeared.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals subtitle B of the Internal Revenue Code, eliminating the estate tax, gift tax, and generation-skipping transfer tax for decedents dying and transfers made after enactment [S3].
The CRS summary confirms the bill's entire subject is repealing these three transfer taxes [S2].

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury — roughly $30 billion a year at the time — which would either come from cuts to other spending, higher taxes elsewhere, or larger deficits borne by general taxpayers. The estate tax applied to fewer than 2% of estates, so the cost of repeal is spread across everyone while the benefit goes to a narrow set of large fortunes.

drawbacks.text: Repeal removes a tax that falls only on the largest inherited fortunes and replaces the revenue either with broader taxes on ordinary taxpayers or with deficits [S2].
The bill had no phase-out, no replacement revenue source, and no cosponsors, indicating no coalition existed to pair repeal with any offset [S4, S5].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is narrow — a small number of very large estates would escape taxation on inherited wealth — while the cost, roughly $30 billion a year in lost revenue at the time, is shared by every federal taxpayer. The bill contained no alternative revenue source, making the trade-off lopsided.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced January 6, 1999 by Rep. Bob Stump and referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day [S5].
No further action was ever recorded; the bill never received a markup, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the 106th Congress ended January 3, 2001 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The estate tax, gift tax, and generation-skipping transfer tax remained in place, so the general taxpayer who would have picked up the cost of repeal is better off; heirs of large fortunes gained nothing from the bill's failure but lost nothing either.

for.name: Rep. Bob Stump
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer taxes on January 6, 1999.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on January 6, 1999 and took no further action on the bill for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, and with zero cosponsors there is no record of partisan support beyond the Republican sponsor [S4].

industries.industry: Heirs and holders of very large estates
industries.note: Repeal would have ended taxation on inherited fortunes above the filing threshold, a benefit flowing almost entirely to the wealthiest families while the lost revenue is made up by general taxpayers [S2].

industries.industry: Estate planning lawyers and tax advisors
industries.note: These professionals earn fees designing trusts and shelters to minimize estate and gift tax exposure; repeal would eliminate much of that business. Their clients would gain, so the industry's loss tracks its clients' gain.
